posts.title: How embassy appointments
posts.excerpt: A clear walkthrough of booking an embassy or consulate appointment, what to bring, and how to avoid the delays that catch most applicants out.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Most embassies and consulates work on an appointment basis. Slots can be limited, so planning ahead and arriving with a complete file makes a real difference to your timeline.

sections.heading: Booking Your Slot
sections.body: Appointments are usually booked through the embassy or an official portal. Choose the correct visa or service category, pay any fee and keep your confirmation, as you will need it at the entrance.
sections.imageAlt: Adviser and clients in a meeting

sections.heading: What to Bring
sections.body: Bring your passport, appointment confirmation, completed forms, photographs and all supporting documents in the order the embassy lists them. Carry originals and copies.

sections.heading: On the Day
sections.body: Arrive early, follow security instructions and answer questions briefly and honestly. Interviews are often short, so be ready to explain your purpose of travel clearly.
sections.imageAlt: Agent reviewing documents with a client

sections.heading: Useful Tips
sections.body: Check the embassy's official website for current rules, avoid third parties who promise guaranteed slots, and keep digital copies of every document you submit.

posts.title: Understanding apostille
posts.excerpt: What apostille and attestation mean, when you need them, and how they help your certificates be accepted by foreign authorities.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: When a document issued in one country is used in another, the receiving authority needs to trust it. Attestation and apostille are the formal ways of providing that assurance.

sections.heading: What Is an Apostille?
sections.body: An apostille is a certificate issued under the Hague Convention that confirms a public document is genuine. Countries that are members of the convention accept it without further embassy legalisation.

sections.heading: When Is Attestation Needed?
sections.body: If the destination country is not part of the convention, documents are usually attested step by step: by the issuing authority, the foreign ministry and finally the destination country's embassy.

sections.heading: Common Documents
sections.body: Educational certificates, birth and marriage certificates, police clearance and commercial documents are the most frequent items that need to be legalised.

sections.heading: Useful Tips
sections.body: Confirm the exact requirement with the receiving authority first, keep originals safe and allow extra time, as ministry and embassy processing can vary.

posts.title: Embassy vs consulate:
posts.excerpt: Both represent a country abroad, but they do different jobs. Learn which one handles your visa, passport or document request.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: People often use the words embassy and consulate interchangeably, but they serve different purposes. Knowing which to approach saves time and avoids misdirected applications.

sections.heading: The Embassy
sections.body: An embassy is the main diplomatica mission, usually located in the capital. It maintains relations between governments and often oversees consular work for the whole country.

sections.heading: The Consulate
sections.body: Consulates are located in other major cities and focus on citizen and visa services: issuing visas, renewing passports and providing assistance to nationals abroad.

sections.heading: Which Should You Contact?
sections.body: For visas and passports, start with the consulate or embassy section responsible for your region. Official websites list jurisdictions and the services each office provides.
sections.imageAlt: National flags hanging from a building

sections.heading: Useful Tips
sections.body: Always use official channels, check opening hours and holidays, and confirm whether your service needs an appointment before travelling to the office.

posts.title: How to prepare for
posts.excerpt: Practical preparation tips to help you stay calm, answer clearly and present a consistent, honest application at the consulate.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: A visa interview is usually short, but it carries weight. Consular officers want to confirm the information in your application and understand your plans.

sections.heading: Know Your Application
sections.body: Re-read your forms and supporting documents before the interview. Your answers should match them exactly, from travel dates to finances and your purpose of visit.
sections.imageAlt: Officials shaking hands at a table

sections.heading: Organise Your Documents
sections.body: Arrange documents in the order the embassy lists them and carry originals as well as copies. A tidy file shows you are well prepared.

sections.heading: During the Interview
sections.body: Answer directly and honestly, and do not volunteer unrelated details. If you do not understand a question, politely ask for it to be repeated.

sections.heading: Useful Tips
sections.body: Dress neatly, arrive early, stay calm and practise common questions beforehand. A mock interview with an adviser can build real confidence.
